reconstructed_theorem_text: For every measurable spaces W and X, with measurable singletons in W, every joint probability measure P on X times R, every kernel K:W->X->R, and a supplied L2(P) membership witness for the actual response z->z.2, let N be any natural number with N>0 and w0,w1:Fin N->W any two indexed particle families. Assume for each j:Fin N that K(w0(j)) and K(w1(j)) belong to L2(PX), where PX=P.map Prod.fst. These supplied memberships mean almost-everywhere strong measurability and finite L2 seminorm under the indicated actual measures. Use the following fixed definitions. Set PX=P.map Prod.fst, the actual first-coordinate marginal. Define rho0=(N:nonnegative_extended_reals)^(-1) times sum_{j:Fin N} dirac(w0(j)) and rho1=(N:nonnegative_extended_reals)^(-1) times sum_{j:Fin N} dirac(w1(j)). For every real t define the actual positive measure curve(t)=ofReal(1-t) times rho0 + ofReal(t) times rho1, where ofReal(r) embeds max(r,0) into the nonnegative extended reals. Define predictor(law,x)=integral_W K(q,x) dlaw(q) for every measure law on W, and risk(law)=integral_{X times R}(predictor(law,z.1)-z.2)^2 dP(z). Define one potential(q)=2*integral_{X times R}(predictor(rho0,z.1)-z.2)*K(q,z.1) dP(z). Abbreviate D=integral_W potential(q) drho1(q)-integral_W potential(q) drho0(q). Every integral is a literal real Bochner integral on the full displayed space with the indicated measure. Then all four outer conclusions hold: (1) For every t in the closed interval [0,1], curve(t) is a probability measure and z->(predictor(curve(t),z.1)-z.2)^2 is genuinely integrable under P. (2) potential is genuinely integrable under rho0. (3) potential is genuinely integrable under rho1. (4) The real function t->risk(curve(t)) has derivative D within [0,1] at its endpoint 0, including its actual value at 0. There are exactly N indices at each endpoint, without a distinctness condition. Repeated particle values, including overlaps between the two families, accumulate their masses. The segment is supported on the finite union of the endpoint particle values. On [0,1] the coefficients are exactly 1-t and t; curve(0)=rho0 and curve(1)=rho1. Each endpoint predictor is the pointwise arithmetic average of its N sampled raw features, and prediction along this finite segment is their affine interpolation. The derivative is the right-hand derivative relative to the closed interval and uses risk(curve(0))=risk(rho0); it is not an unrestricted two-sided derivative of the clipped extension. The response is the actual second coordinate of P, with no independence or product decomposition assumed. Supplied label and sampled-feature L2 memberships yield the displayed squared-loss and endpoint potential integrability conclusions. No uniform feature norm bound is supplied. Only sampled slices carry feature membership assumptions; no global measurability or L2 assumption on the whole kernel is imposed. For q in the finite endpoint support, the inner potential integrand is genuinely P-integrable by these sampled L2 assumptions. For q outside that support, no such integrability is asserted, so the formula defining potential retains its totalized real-integral meaning there. Potential integrability under the two empirical laws and the derivative statement do not give a genuine global first variation at arbitrary off-support locations or under arbitrary parameter laws. Both scalar integrals in D use the same rho0-anchored potential, with rho1 minus rho0 direction; this is not an integral against positive or truncated subtraction of measures. The risk is the unhalved integrated squared residual, so potential has literal factor 2. The full conclusion has the segment assertion, two endpoint scalar integrability assertions, and the endpoint derivative; no quantitative remainder budget is part of it.
